pearls.title: Methicillin-Resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA)
pearls.body_text:
MRSA Definition: Methicillin MIC 8 µg/ml or more, Oxacillin MIC 4 µg/ml or more.

Resistance in MRSA is mediated by mecA gene which is chromosomally coded.

It alters PBP (penicillin binding protein) present on s.aureus cell wall to PBP-2a which has less affinity for beta-lactam antibiotics.

Penicillin Binding Protein:
• Normal protein present in all bacterial cell wall.
• Transpeptidase in nature.
• Required for cross-linking of the peptidoglycan layer (essential for cell wall synthesis).
• It is also the site of attachment for- beta-lactam drugs to bind & inhibit.

Types of MRSA:
• Community-acquired - mediated by mec A subtype IV and Possess PV Toxin(Panton-Valentine Toxin), monodrug resistance,more virulent
• Hospital-acquired - mediated by mec A subtype I, II, III, multidrug resistance,less virulent.

Detection of MRSA:
• Antibiotic susceptibility test on Muller Hilton agar (Disk diffusion test) by using Methicillin or Oxacillin disc or cefoxitin disc.
• PCR for detection of mecA gene.

Conditions to be maintained for Incubation:
• On media containing 4% NaCl
• Incubation at 30°C
• Full 24hr incubation

Treatment:
• Vancomycin is Drug Of Choice (should be used only if other drugs are resistant ).
• Others- Teicoplanin, Linezolid, streptogramin, cipro/levofloxacin, cotrimoxazole, clindamycin, mupirocin, minocycline.
• Newer Drugs – Daptomycin, ceftobiprole, tigecycline, oritavancin,dalbavancin,telavancin,delaflc [delafloxacin]
• Ceftobiprole and ceftaroline are 5th generation β lactams effective against MRSA.

question_stem.text: By which of the following ways penicillin resistance is commonly transferred in Staphylococcus aureus?
question_stem.markdown: By which of the following ways penicillin resistance is commonly transferred in Staphylococcus aureus?

peer_accuracy_statement: 60% of the people got this right
explanation_markdown:
Penicillin resistance in *Staphylococcus aureus* determined by plasmids that are transferred by **transduction (most common method) followed by conjugation.**

**Conjugation** is the most common method of antibiotic resistance transfer in most of the other bacteria.

**Genetic transfer** is the mechanism by which DNA is transferred from a donor to a recipient.

In bacteria, genetic transfer of resistance can occur in the following ways:
1.Transformation
2.Transduction
3.Conjugation

**Transformation:** After death or cell lysis, some bacteria release their DNA into the environment. Other bacteria, generally of the same species, can come into contact with these fragments, take them up and incorporate them into their DNA by recombination.

**Transduction:** This method involves the transfer of DNA, episome or plasmid from one bacterium to another with the use of a bacteriophage (phage).

**Conjugation:** This mechanism requires the presence of a special plasmid called the F plasmid (that codes for sex pilus) through the formation of temporary cytoplasmic bridge.

images.caption: Slide coagulase test showing positive clumping in circle 5 (left) and negative homogeneous suspension in circle 6 (right)
images.visual_description: Photograph of a glass slide with two circular wax rings labeled '5' (left, showing coarse macroscopic clumping/agglutination of staphylococci) and '6' (right, showing smooth milky unagglutinated suspension).

images.caption: Tube coagulase test showing positive fibrin clot (+) vs. negative liquid plasma (-)
images.visual_description: Photograph of two horizontal glass test tubes: the top tube (labeled '+') shows a solid coagulated fibrin clot that remains in place when tilted, and the bottom tube (labeled '-') shows uncoagulated liquid plasma.

explanation_markdown:
The given image is of positive slide coagulase test which is not seen with *Staphylococcus schleiferi* .

**Coagulase test** is used to differentiate *Staphylococcus aureus* (positive) from coagulase-negative *Staphylococcus* (CONS).

**Coagulase** is an enzyme produced by *S. aureus* that **converts (soluble) fibrinogen in plasma to (insoluble) fibrin.**

*Staphylococcus aureus* produces two forms of coagulase, **bound and free.**

**1. Slide coagulase test** is done to detect **bound coagulase or clumping factor** and **does not require coagulase-reacting factor (CRF)** in plasma.
• Clumping factor directly **converts fibrinogen to fibrin**.
• It **cross-links α and β chain of fibrinogen** in plasma to form fibrin clot that gets deposited on the cell wall of the cocci.
• As a result, individual coccus sticks to each other and clumping can be observed.
• Heavy suspension of the organism is made on glass slide and mixed with drop of plasma
• Agglutination indicates a positive test:
  ◦ Indicates *S. aureus*
  ◦ Some species of coagulase-negative *Staphylococcus* can be positive

**Note: All coagulase-negative slides must be confirmed using tube coagulase test as the definitive test for *S. aureus*.**

**2. Tube coagulase test** is done to detect **free coagulase** and **requires coagulase-reacting factor (CRF)in plasma.**
• Detects staphylocoagulase which **reacts with coagulase-reacting factor (CRF)**
• CRF is a thrombin-like molecule
• Staphylocoagulase and CRF combine to **indirectly convert fibrinogen to fibrin.**
• A suspension of the organism is suspended and incubated with plasma at 37°C
• **Clot formation within 4 hours** indicates a positive test
  ◦ Positive test indicates *S. aureus*
  ◦ Some species of coagulase-negative *Staphylococcus* can be positive
• Negative tubes should be held overnight at room temp.
  ◦ Some species possess enzyme that can cause dissolution of clot after prolonged incubation

**Both slide and tube coagulase positive:**
• *S. aureus*

• They are often situated at the poles of the granules and called **polar bodies.**
• **Albert's stain, Neisser's stain**, and **Ponder's stain** are used to demonstrate the metachromatic granules (Volutin/Babes Ernst granules) of ***Corynebacterium diphtheria*.**
• The bacilli are usually arranged in pairs or palisades or small groups, at various angles to each other, resembling the **letters V or L.**
• This has been called the **Chinese letter or cuneiform arrangement.**
• This is due to the incomplete separation of daughter cells after binary fission.

question_stem.text: Diphtheria toxin resembles which other toxin in its mechanism of action?
question_stem.markdown: Diphtheria toxin resembles which other toxin in its mechanism of action?

peer_accuracy_statement: 40% of the people got this right
explanation_markdown:
Both **diphtheria toxin** and **pseudomonas exotoxin** act by inhibiting **elongation factor, EF-2**

**Mechanism of action of diphtheria toxin:**
• Diphtheria toxin is a protein and consists of **two fragments, A & B.**
• Both the fragments are necessary for the toxic effect.
• When released by the bacterium the toxin is inactive, as the active site on the fragment A is masked.
• Activation is accomplished by the **protease enzyme** present in the culture medium or infected host tissues.
• All the **enzymatic activity** is present in **fragment A** whereas **fragment B helps the toxin to bind** to the cells.
• Diphtheria toxin acts by **inhibiting protein synthesis.**
• Specifically, fragment A of diphtheria exotoxin is responsible, which inhibits polypeptide chain elongation in the presence of **nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide** by inhibiting the **elongation factor EF2.**

Note: ADP ribosylation is one of the methods of modification of proteins. Both pseudomonas exotoxin A and diphteria toxin act by inhibiting the **EF-2** by its ADP ribosylation. ADP ribosylation of **other proteins** is responsible for the action of other toxins,e.g. cholera toxin.

pearls.title: Mechanism of action of various bacterial toxins
pearls.body_text:
The mechanism of action of various bacterial toxins are as given below:

1. Adenylate cyclase
• Adenylate cyclase toxin (Bordetella spp.)
• Edema factor (Bacillus anthracis)
• Exotoxin Y (Pseudomonas aeruginosa)

2. ADP-Ribosylation
• Cholera toxin (Vibrio cholerae)
• Heat-labile toxin (Escherichia coli)
• Diphtheria toxin (Corynebacterium diphtheriae)
• Exotoxin A (Pseudomonas aeruginosa)
• Pertussis toxin (Bordetella pertussis)
• C2 toxin and C3 ADP-ribosyltransferase (Clostridium botulinum)

3. Deamidation
• Cytotoxic necrotizing factor (Escherichia coli)
• Dermonecrotic toxin (Bordetella pertussis)

4. Glucosylation
• Toxin A and B (Clostridium difficile)

5. Metalloproteinase
• Lethal factor (Bacillus anthracis)
• Enterotoxin (Bacteroides fragilis)
• Botulinum neurotoxin (Clostridium botulinum)
• Tetanus neurotoxin (Clostridium tetani)

6. RNA glycosidase
• Shiga toxin (Shigella dysenteriae)
• Shiga-like toxin (Escherichia coli)

Note :
Cyclic AMP inducers ("CAPE")
• Cholera toxin => ADP-R of Gs
• Anthrax: Edema factor => AC
• Pertussis toxin => ADP-R of Gi
• E. coli: Heat-labile toxin 1 => ADP-R of Gs

question_stem.markdown: Lysogenic conversion is seen in

peer_accuracy_statement: 91% of the people got this right
explanation_markdown:
Lysogenic conversion is seen in diphtheria.

• The **toxigenicity** of **diphtheria bacillus** depends on the presence of the **corynephages (tox+)**, which acts as the genetic determinant controlling the toxin production.
• Non-toxigenic strains may be rendered toxigenic by infecting them with beta phage or some other phage.
• This is known as **lysogenic or phage conversion.**
• The toxigenicity remains only as long as the bacillus is lysogenic.
• When the bacillus is cured of its phage, by growing it in the presence of antiphage serum, it loses the toxigenic capacity.

Lysogenic conversion:
• Cholera toxin
• Diptheria toxin
• Verocytotoxin
• Botulinum toxin-C and D
• Panton valentine toxin
• Streptococcal pyogenic exotoxin-A and C

question_stem.markdown: Toxin production of diphtheria bacilli depends on

options.text: Concentration of iron in the medium

peer_accuracy_statement: 70% of the people got this right
explanation_markdown:
Toxin production of diphtheria bacilli depends on the concentration of iron in the medium, tox phage, and biotype.

• **Diphtheria toxin (DT)** production **decreases with increase in iron concentration.**
• Presence of increased concentration of **iron increases the DT represser gene** thereby decreasing toxin production.
• **Optimum level of iron** for toxin production is **0.14 µg/millilitre**, while a concentration of 0.5 µg/milliliter inhibits the formation of toxins.
• Toxin production also depends on the **3 biotypes** and is **coded by phage (corynebacteriophage tox+).**
• DT is also produced by *Corynebacterium ulcerans* and *Corynebacterium pseudotuberculosis*

peer_accuracy_statement: 66% of the people got this right

images.caption: Schematic diagram of Elek's gel precipitation test showing filter paper strip with C. diphtheriae antitoxin, horizontal bacterial streaks, and 45-degree precipitin lines
images.visual_description: Schematic diagram of an agar plate containing a vertical 'Filter paper strip with C. diphtheriae antitoxin' crossed perpendicularly by three horizontal bacterial streaks: top 'Known toxigenic C. diphtheriae' (with diagonal 'Precipitin line' arcs), middle 'Unknown (pt's isolate)' (showing coalescing diagonal precipitin lines indicating toxigenicity), and bottom 'Known nontoxigenic C. diphtheriae' (no precipitin lines).
embedded_text_and_labels: Filter paper strip with C. diphtheriae antitoxin

explanation_markdown:
**Elek test** is an in vitro **immunoprecipitation (immunodiffusion) test** to determine whether or not a strain of ***Corynebacterium diphtheriae*** is toxigenic (For checking susceptibility to diphtheria **Schick test** is used).

**Procedure of Elek test:**
• A test strip of filter paper containing diphtheria antitoxin is placed in the center of the agar plate. Strains to be tested (patient's isolate), as well as known positive and negative toxigenic strains, are streaked on the agar's surface in a line across the plate and at a right angle to the antitoxin paper strip.
• Antitoxin diffuses away from the strip of filter paper, whereas toxin produced by toxin-producing strains diffuse away from growth. At the zone of equivalence, a precipitin line is formed.
• After 24 hours of incubation at 37°C, the plate is examined with transmitted light for the presence of fine precipitin lines at a 45-degree angle to the streaks.

**Positive Test:**
• If precipitin lines are formed at the zone of equivalence, the test organism is toxigenic.
• If the toxin is produced by the test strain, it diffuses sideways from the streak.
• The antitoxin diffuses from the filter paper, and a precipitin line formed where the toxin and the antitoxin meet (at zone of equivalence).
• The control strain also will cause the formation of a precipitate, which will coalesce with the precipitate of the test strain to form a line of identity.

explanation_markdown:
The formation of pseudomembrane on the posterior pharynx is characteristic feature of diphtheria.

• The **diphtheria bacilli** remain confined to the site of entry, where they multiply and form the toxin.
• The toxin causes **local necrotic changes** and the resulting fibrinous exudate, together with the disintegrating epithelial cells, leukocytes, erythrocytes, and bacteria, constitute the **pseudomembrane**, which is **characteristic of diphtheritic infection.**
• **Removal** of the membrane reveals a **bleeding**, edematous mucosa.
• The distribution of the membrane varies from local (e.g., tonsillar, pharyngeal) to widely covering the entire tracheobronchial tree.
• The membrane is intensely infectious, and droplet and contact precautions must be followed when examining or caring for infected patients.

question_stem.markdown: Erythrasma is caused by

peer_accuracy_statement: 78% of the people got this right
explanation_markdown:
The causative organism of erythrasma is ***Corynebacterium minutissimum***, which usually is present as a normal human skin inhabitant.

**Erythrasma** is a chronic superficial infection of the **intertriginous areas** (axilla, anogenital regions, skin folds of breast, etc.) of the skin.

The bacterium is a **lipophilic, gram-positive**, non-spore-forming, aerobic, and **catalase-positive diphtheroid.**

**Predisposing factors for erythrasma include the following:**
• Excessive sweating/hyperhidrosis
• Delicate cutaneous barrier
• Obesity
• Diabetes mellitus
• Warm climate
• Poor hygiene
• Advanced age
• Other immunocompromised states

The **stratum corneum is thickened.** The organisms that cause erythrasma are seen in the intercellular spaces as well as within cells, dissolving keratin fibrils.

The **coral-red fluorescence** of scales seen under **Wood light** is secondary to the production of porphyrin by these diphtheroids.

The typical appearance of erythrasma is well-demarcated, **brown-red macular patches.**

• *C. jeikeium* is a **"lipophilic"** bacterial species, meaning its **growth is generally enhanced by the presence of lipids.**

images.caption: Schematic diagram of Listeria monocytogenes intracellular lifecycle and cell-to-cell spread via InlA/InlB, LLO, ActA, and PlcA/PlcB
images.visual_description: Schematic diagram showing a Listeria rod binding host cell surface via 'InlA, InlB' -> 'entry' into a vacuole -> 'LLO' mediating 'vacuolar lysis' -> intracellular 'replication' -> 'ActA' inducing 'actin-based motility' (red actin comet tail) -> filopod protrusion mediating 'cell-to-cell spread' into an adjacent host cell -> 'LLO, PlcA, PlcB' mediating double-membrane 'vacuolar lysis'.

explanation_markdown:
*Listeria* moves from cell-to-cell using host cell actin framework.

• *Listeria monocytogenes* enters the body through the GIT after ingestion of contaminated food such as **cheese or vegetables.**
• It has two cell-surface proteins, **internalins A and B**, which interact with the **epithelial E-cadherin** and promote its own **phagocytosis into the gut epithelial cells.**
• In the phagolysosome, the **low pH activates** the bacterium to produce **listeriolysin O.**
• This enzyme **lyses the membrane of the phagolysosome** and allows *Listeria* to **escape into the cytoplasm** of the epithelial cell.
• Here, the organisms **proliferate and produce ActA**, a listerial protein which **induces host cell actin polymerization.**
• This process **propels them to the host cell membrane.**
• Pushing against the host cell membrane, they cause the formation of **elongated protrusions called filopods.**
• These **filopods are ingested by adjacent epithelial cells**, macrophages, and hepatocytes, the listeriae are released & the cycle begins again.
• In this way, ***Listeria* moves from cell-to-cell using host actin framework without being exposed to antibodies, complement system, or neutrophils.**

explanation_markdown:
**Tetanus toxin** has similar mechanisms of action as strychnine but **acts pre-synaptically.**

**Strychnine** prevents the uptake of glycine at inhibitory synapses **post-synaptically**, especially in the ventral horns (anterior horn cells) of the spinal cord.

**Mechanism of action of tetanus toxin:**

• **Tetanolysin:** No role in pathogenesis

Both these toxins **cause spastic muscle contractions** by blocking the action of inhibitory neurotransmitters.

The mechanism of action **botulinum toxins** is different as it **prevents the release of acetylcholine**, thereby causing decreased muscle tone and paralysis.

• Metronidazole (DOC) preferred over Penicillin for 7 days (start within 6 hours of infection). Metronidazole (500 mg every six hours intravenously or by mouth); Penicillin G (100,000–200,000 IU/kg/day intravenously, given in 2–4 divided doses).

Symptomatic treatment- Antispasmodic.
